archived.verdict_explanation: Supported: (1) 1-month postoperative CRP and IL-6 medians (IQRs) and P-values; (2) CRP remained significantly elevated through 12-month follow-up; (3) Figure 4 reports the stated inverse correlations with rs (as 'Spearman's coefficient'), R2, P-values, and N for grip strength and SF-36 PCS. Not supported as written: (a) IL-6 persistence 'through 12 months'—the text only states IL-6 remained significantly increased at 3- and 6-month follow-ups; (b) the multivariable regression claim lacks the requested model details and p-value in the provided source text and instead cites Table S6 (supplementary, not included here). Also, the candidate’s 'surged' phrasing is not used in the source; the source states '4.8-fold increase' and '4.2-fold increase.'
archived.readiness_reason: All requested statistics (N, coefficient, R2, P) are explicitly stated in the figure caption.
archived.original_claim: Vogel et al. (2023) report that one month post-operatively CRP increased 4.8-fold to 0.48 mg/dL (0.14–0.90) vs 0.10 mg/dL (0.06–0.39) during active Cushing’s syndrome (P≤0.001) and IL-6 increased 4.2-fold to 7.2 pg/mL (3.3–11.7) vs 1.7 pg/mL (1.5–2.5) (P≤0.001), with elevations persisting through 12 months. They also report that 3-month CRP inversely correlated with 12-month normalized hand grip strength (rs=−0.371, R2=0.155, P=0.008, N=50) and SF-36 PCS (rs=−0.356, R2=0.127, P=0.028, N=38), and that multivariable linear regression found 3-month CRP independently predicted 12-month grip strength after adjusting for age and BMI (P<0.05).
